title: The ten-day course
hook: S. N. Goenka's ten-day silent courses in the method of U Ba Khin, offered on donations

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newar Buddhism, where the priest at the shrine is also somebody's father. Your line was the valley's way. What did the older person you asked remember? Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

At the front desk you hand over your phone. Your books go too, and your notebook, and your pen. Someone shows you to a simple room and a cushion in a quiet hall. For the next ten days you will not talk with the person on the next cushion, or catch their eye, or pass them a note. You will sit, eat plain food, walk, sleep, and sit again. And when it is over and you walk back to the desk, nobody hands you a bill. People sign up for this, again and again. Today: the ten-day course.
screen: `HAND OVER THE PHONE.` → `NO TALKING, NO NOTES.` → `NO BILL AT THE END.`

segments.voice: First, the teachers. S. N. Goenka was born into an Indian family in Burma, now Myanmar, and became a businessman there. He learned meditation from U Ba Khin, a Burmese lay teacher who also served in his country's government. Goenka later began teaching in India, and the courses spread from there to centers around the world, taught in the same form in each place, with his recorded instructions guiding the students. Second, the silence. The courses ask for noble silence: no speaking, gestures or messages between students, so that each person is left alone with their own mind. A student may still speak with the teacher about the practice, and with the staff about practical needs. Third, the method. The course begins with the breath, attention resting on the small area around the nostrils, feeling the air come and go, just as it is. When the mind has steadied, attention moves through the whole body, part by part, noticing sensations: warmth, pressure, tingling, ache. The instruction is to observe them without grasping at the pleasant ones or pushing away the unpleasant ones, and to see that each one arises and passes. The Pali word for that passing is anicca, impermanence. On the final day comes metta, loving kindness, and the silence is lifted. Goenka presented the method as belonging to no sect, a practice anyone could try without converting to anything. Fourth, the money, or the lack of it. There is no charge for teaching, food or lodging. Courses run on donations from people who have already completed one and want someone else to have the same chance. Every student sits, in a sense, as the guest of a stranger who came before.
screen: `FROM U BA KHIN TO GOENKA.` · `NOBLE SILENCE.` · `FIRST THE BREATH, THEN THE BODY.` · `OFFERED ON DONATIONS.` · then, large: `TEN DAYS OF SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here is a small taste of the method. Sit with your back upright and your eyes closed. Bring attention to the small area just below the nostrils, above the upper lip. Feel the breath touch there, in and out. Don't control it; just notice it, natural, as it is. When the mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself. Near the end, let your attention move once, slowly, from the top of the head down to the toes, noticing whatever sensation is there and letting it pass. And if you'd like, choose one time this week to sit for a full hour. The bell holds the time.
The ten-day course. The silent meditation courses taught by S. N. Goenka in the method of U Ba Khin: breath, then body, offered free and funded by donations. Today's word.
Your line: ten days of silence. Today, take ten minutes of silence instead: no talking, no screen, no notes, and see what the mind does with the space. Day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Students at S. N. Goenka's courses keep noble silence for ten days, practicing attention to the breath and then to sensations throughout the body; the courses charge no fee and are funded by donations from past students.

fork.setup: it's the middle of the course. your knee aches and a pleasant warmth spreads through your hands. what does the method ask?
options: chase the warmth and ignore the knee.
observe both, grasping at neither, and see each one pass.
stop sitting until the ache is gone.
fork.reveal: observe without grasping or pushing away. the point is to see that every sensation arises and passes: anicca.

original.note: Pali anicca, impermanence: what the ten-day course asks students to see in every sensation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silent retreat is a quiet vacation.
what it means: ten days of noble silence, working with the breath and then the body's sensations, offered free.
what a scholar hears: a Burmese lay teaching line from U Ba Khin to Goenka, presented as non-sectarian, centered on seeing anicca in sensation.

notes: Biographical details (Goenka born in Burma to an Indian family, a businessman; U Ba Khin a lay teacher who served in the Burmese government): confirm.
Course structure stated without counts (breath first, then body, metta on the final day when silence lifts): confirm against the code of discipline.
Practice mentions sitting 'a full hour' because the outline's practice is 'sit one hour'; courses include hour-long sittings, not stated as a number of sittings.
'Presented the method as belonging to no sect' paraphrases Goenka's non-sectarian framing; confirm.
Hook scene is a composite illustration of a course arrival, not a specific center.
Editor: practice no longer tells the listener their mind will wander ('and it will' cut).
